briefOverview: Ezekiel records a second, detailed vision of the cherubim, their wheels, and the departure of the divine glory from the temple. The chapter also depicts a man taking coals from between the cherubim to scatter over the city, signaling judgment.
summary: The prophet sees a throne-like sapphire expanse above the cherubim and is commanded to have a man clothed in linen take coals of fire from between the cherubim to scatter over the city (vv. 1–3). The cherubim stand on the right side of the temple as a cloud fills the inner court and the glory of the LORD moves from the cherub to the temple threshold (vv. 3–5). One cherub hands fire to the man in linen, who takes it and goes out (vv. 6–7). Ezekiel then describes in detail the four wheels beside each cherub — wheels within wheels, full of eyes — and the fourfold faces (cherub, man, lion, eagle) common to the living creatures (vv. 9–15). The cherubim and wheels move together under the control of the creatures' heads and the spirit of the living creatures (vv. 11–17). Finally, the glory departs the threshold, stands over the cherubim, and the cherubim lift up and station themselves at the east gate of the LORD's house; the prophet identifies these beings as the same living creatures he saw earlier by the Chebar river (vv. 18–22).
externalContext: Ezekiel was a priestly prophet among the Judean exiles in Babylon in the early sixth century BCE; many of his visions interpret the fate of Jerusalem and the temple from the perspective of exile. The motifs here — cherubim, throne-chariot (merkavah) imagery, wheels within wheels, and the cloud/glory (kabod) of YHWH — draw on Israelite temple and cultic vocabulary and likely engage broader ancient Near Eastern throne symbolism. Fire commonly signifies divine judgment or purification in prophetic literature, so the coals taken to be scattered over the city fit Ezekiel’s broader theme of impending judgment.
externalReferences: This chapter closely parallels and develops the vision in Ezekiel 1 (see Ezekiel 1:4–28 and 1:15–21 for the same living creatures and wheels imagery). The theme of the glory of the LORD departing the temple is continued and summarized elsewhere in Ezekiel, especially Ezekiel 8–11 and explicitly in Ezekiel 11:22–23. The image of cherubim associated with the divine throne and presence also echoes temple lore such as Exodus 25:18–22 (cherubim on the ark) and finds thematic resonance with other throne visions like Isaiah 6:1–4 and the living creatures of Revelation 4:6–8.
practicalQuestions: If God's presence can 'depart' from a worship space in Ezekiel, how should contemporary communities think about the relationship between holiness and corporate behavior?
What do symbols like fire, wheels, and cherubim communicate about divine authority, and how might they shape worship or moral urgency today?
How should modern readers balance awe and fear when encountering powerful, transcendent biblical imagery?
In what practical ways can communities respond to warnings of judgment while also seeking restoration or reform?
uncertainAreas: The text does not explicitly identify the 'man clothed with linen' (priestly agent, angelic attendant, or symbolic figure), nor does it spell out precisely whether the coals scattered over the city indicate immediate physical destruction, ritual purification, or symbolic judgment. The function of the many eyes on the wheels (whether vigilance, knowledge, or a poetic way to express divine omniscience/mobility) is also open to interpretation.
